name: Redensyl

angle.text: Users apply Redensyl serums to thinning areas hoping for fuller hair and a denser-looking hairline. It is promoted as a cosmetic alternative or add-on to drug treatments. Evidence for this use comes from small, industry-linked product studies.

summary: A patented plant-and-zinc blend in anti-hair-loss serums; small, industry-linked product studies, no approved-drug status.
note: Human studies tested multi-ingredient products, not Redensyl alone.
currentQuick:
Redensyl is a cosmetic ingredient used in over-the-counter hair serums. Its maker says it reactivates dormant follicle stem cells.
Small studies of products containing it report improvements, but they test blends, are short, and often have industry-linked authors.
How it works: Claimed to stimulate follicle stem and outer root sheath cells via Wnt-related signalling; support described is from lab and ex vivo work.
Risks and caveats: Reported adverse events in the small studies were none significant. It is a cosmetic, not an approved hair-loss drug; allergy patch-testing is advised for plant-sensitive people per Grokipedia.
deepLead:
Redensyl is a patented cosmetic active ingredient for anti-hair-loss serums and lotions, developed by Givaudan Active Beauty (formerly Induchem). According to Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, it combines a larch-derived dihydroquercetin glucoside, a green tea derivative (EGCG2), glycine and zinc chloride, and is used at roughly 1 to 3 percent. 
The manufacturer-style claim is that it reactivates dormant hair follicle stem cells; the supporting data described in that source are in vitro or ex vivo.  Published human studies are small and typically test finished products that contain Redensyl together with other actives, often with industry-linked authors. 
Redensyl is regulated as a cosmetic ingredient rather than a drug, so products carrying it are not approved to treat hair loss.

name: Capixyl

angle.text: Capixyl serums are used by people with thinning hair who want a denser look without prescription drugs. Promoters say the peptide and red clover blend supports follicles. Evidence for that use rests mostly on supplier data and tests of the combination.

summary: A peptide and red clover blend in hair serums; claims rest mostly on supplier data and combination tests.
note: No independent single-ingredient human trial found.
currentQuick:
Capixyl is a cosmetic ingredient combining a peptide with red clover extract, sold for use in anti-hair-loss serums.
The supplier cites reduced shedding, but the available sources give few independent human data.
How it works: Claimed to improve follicle anchoring via collagen and laminin, and to inhibit 5-alpha reductase through biochanin A; lab-level support cited by Grokipedia is at high concentrations.
Risks and caveats: No specific adverse effects are documented in the sources; it is regulated as a cosmetic and is not an approved treatment for hair loss.
deepLead:
Capixyl is a trademarked cosmetic active ingredient from Lucas Meyer Cosmetics, now part of Clariant, used in hair-loss serums. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, describes it as a combination of the peptide acetyl tetrapeptide-3 with red clover (Trifolium pratense) flower extract standardized for the isoflavone biochanin A. 
The supplier claims it reduces shedding by anchoring follicles, moderating DHT and limiting inflammation.  The sources found offer few independent human data: much of the quoted efficacy comes from supplier material or from tests of a three-ingredient combination rather than Capixyl alone.

name: Procapil

angle.text: Procapil serums are used by people with thinning or shedding hair who want a fuller appearance. It is promoted as a cosmetic active that supports follicles. Evidence for that use is small trials, some run by the sponsor.

summary: A peptide, apigenin and oleanolic acid blend in hair serums; small trials, some sponsor-run, no approved-drug status.
note: Most studies combine it with PRP or other actives.
currentQuick:
Procapil is a cosmetic hair-serum ingredient from Sederma. It combines a biotin-linked peptide with apigenin and oleanolic acid.
Small studies report modest changes, but many are sponsor-run or combine it with other treatments.
How it works: Claimed to anchor follicles, boost scalp microcirculation and reduce DHT effects; these are manufacturer claims per Grokipedia.
Risks and caveats: Tolerability was good in the 4-month trial described; itching and contact dermatitis were reported in a combined PRP study. It is regulated as a cosmetic, not as a drug.
deepLead:
Procapil is a patented cosmetic ingredient from Sederma (Croda) that combines biotinoyl tripeptide-1, apigenin and oleanolic acid. It is used in hair serums marketed against thinning and shedding. 
The supplier claims it anchors follicles, improves scalp microcirculation and limits DHT effects.  Human data are small: a sponsor-commissioned placebo-controlled trial and several investigator studies, many combining Procapil with platelet-rich plasma or other ingredients.

name: Copper peptide scalp serum

angle.text: Hair-loss communities add copper peptide serums to topical stacks, aiming for thicker hair and a denser hairline. The idea draws on GHK-Cu's role in skin repair. No published scalp trials test it for hair growth, so the link rests on theory and anecdote.

summary: GHK-Cu peptide serum for the scalp: popular in hair stacks, with no published scalp trials behind it.
note: Skin evidence is small and short; no scalp hair trials found.
currentQuick:
Copper peptide scalp serums put GHK-Cu, a small copper-binding peptide found naturally in the body, on the scalp. They are marketed for hair thickness and loss prevention.
Most GHK-Cu research is in cell and animal studies, with a few small facial-skin studies. No scalp hair-loss trials were found.
How it works: Proposed actions include supporting wound healing, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, and stimulating collagen and blood vessel growth; none of these have been shown for hair in published human trials.
Risks and caveats: Sold as a cosmetic ingredient. The source notes GHK-Cu also raises matrix metalloproteinases and advises caution; scalp-specific safety data are not available.
deepLead:
A copper peptide scalp serum is a topical cosmetic product containing GHK-Cu (copper tripeptide-1), a complex of the tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine and copper(II), applied to the scalp with the aim of supporting hair growth or thickness.
GHK-Cu occurs naturally in human plasma, saliva and urine, and was isolated from plasma by Loren Pickart in 1973. It is widely used in cosmetics for anti-aging and hair-loss-prevention claims, where it is listed as copper tripeptide-1. Most of the wound-healing evidence cited for GHK-Cu comes from cell cultures and animal studies, and the facial-skin studies that exist are described as small and short.
No clinical studies of scalp copper peptide serums for hair loss were identified for this article.

name: Topical melatonin hair

angle.text: Some people with androgenetic alopecia apply melatonin to the scalp hoping to slow thinning and keep a fuller head of hair. It is an off-label idea drawn from its antioxidant properties. Small trials have looked at it for this use, and it is not an established treatment.

summary: Melatonin solution on the scalp for androgenetic alopecia: a small-trial idea, not an established treatment.
note: Evidence base not confirmed in this entry; check primary trials.
currentQuick:
Melatonin is the sleep-timing hormone; some hair-loss users apply it as a scalp solution.
This entry found general pharmacology only and no loaded trial data, so no effectiveness conclusion is stated.
How it works: Melatonin acts on MT1/MT2 receptors and has antioxidant effects in vitro; its role in hair follicles was not documented in the sources used.
Risks and caveats: Melatonin is sold over the counter as a supplement in many countries; scalp-specific safety data were not reviewed.
deepLead:
Topical melatonin for hair refers to melatonin solutions applied to the scalp in an effort to treat androgenetic alopecia. Melatonin is a hormone made mainly by the pineal gland that regulates sleep-wake timing, and it is also an in vitro antioxidant.
Melatonin has been examined in small studies as a scalp solution, but this article draws only on general reference information about the compound; no trial publications were loaded, so findings are not summarised here.

name: Azelaic acid scalp

angle.text: Hair-loss forum users add azelaic acid to scalp stacks, believing it mildly blocks 5-alpha-reductase like finasteride does, to slow thinning. The enzyme claim comes from lab work. It is studied for acne and rosacea, and no scalp trials test it for pattern hair loss.

summary: Acne/rosacea acid with a lab-only 5-ARI claim, used in hair stacks without scalp trials for pattern hair loss.
note: 5-ARI claim is in vitro only.
currentQuick:
Azelaic acid is a skin treatment for acne and rosacea. Some hair-loss users put it on the scalp for a claimed mild finasteride-like effect.
The claim comes from a 1988 lab study; no pattern-hair-loss trials were found.
How it works: It reduces bacteria, inflammation and pigment production; 5-alpha-reductase inhibition was shown in vitro in combination with zinc sulfate.
Risks and caveats: Dryness and irritation are the main reported effects.
deepLead:
Azelaic acid is a dicarboxylic acid used topically at 15 to 20 percent for acne, rosacea and hyperpigmentation. In hair-loss communities it is sometimes applied to the scalp or added to anti-hair-loss stacks because of claims that it mildly inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, the enzyme targeted by finasteride and dutasteride.
Wikipedia cites a 1988 in vitro report in which azelaic acid combined with zinc sulfate strongly inhibited 5-alpha-reductase in human skin; the article notes this is a single in vitro study and not clinical evidence that topical azelaic acid alone has this effect in vivo. A small early phase 1 trial of azelaic acid in central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA), a scarring alopecia, is registered.

name: Tretinoin for scalp

angle.text: Users mix tretinoin into minoxidil, believing it improves absorption and gives fuller regrowth. It is an approved acne retinoid used here off-label. Evidence for the hair use is described as weak and contradictory.

summary: Retinoid mixed into minoxidil to boost absorption; evidence described as weak and contradictory.
note: Irritation and sun sensitivity; one case report of scalp infection with a combo lotion.
currentQuick:
Tretinoin is a prescription acne and anti-aging retinoid. Some hair-loss users add it to minoxidil.
Reference sources call the evidence weak and contradictory.
How it works: Proposed to raise minoxidil sulfation and scalp penetration.
Risks and caveats: Irritation, peeling and sun sensitivity are common; oral forms carry pregnancy warnings.
deepLead:
Tretinoin (all-trans retinoic acid) is a topical retinoid approved for acne and widely studied for photoaging. In hair-loss communities it is sometimes applied to the scalp or mixed with minoxidil on the theory that it improves minoxidil absorption.
Wikipedia describes the proposed idea as tretinoin helping minoxidil convert to its active sulfate form and penetrate the scalp, and characterises the evidence as weak and contradictory.

name: Cetirizine topical

angle.text: Topical cetirizine is explored as a hair-loss lotion on the theory that blocking prostaglandin D2 signalling protects follicles from shrinking. It is an allergy drug used off-label for this. It has been tested in a small trial in women, and results are not confirmed.

summary: Antihistamine lotion tested in a small female hair-loss trial; results not confirmed here.
note: Topical use is investigational.
currentQuick:
Cetirizine is a common oral allergy drug. A topical version was tested in 66 women with androgenetic alopecia.
Results were not available to this entry.
How it works: Blocks H1 receptors; the hair rationale involves PGD2-related inflammation.
Risks and caveats: Oral cetirizine can cause drowsiness; topical scalp safety was not reviewed.
deepLead:
Topical cetirizine is a lotion form of the second-generation antihistamine cetirizine, tested for androgenetic alopecia based on the idea that prostaglandin D2 (PGD2) contributes to hair-follicle miniaturisation.
A phase 2/3 trial, NCT04481412, in 66 women with androgenetic alopecia was completed after starting in 2020; no results were loaded for this article.

name: Setipiprant

angle.text: Setipiprant is followed in hair-loss circles as an investigational drug that targets prostaglandin D2, which is elevated in balding scalp. It began as an allergy and asthma drug. In its phase 2a hair trial it did not beat placebo.

summary: PGD2-receptor blocker that came from allergy research to hair loss, and did not beat placebo in its phase 2a trial.
note: Never approved; hair trial reported no significant benefit.
currentQuick:
Setipiprant is an experimental oral drug that blocks the PGD2 receptor CRTH2. It was developed for asthma and hay fever, then tested for male pattern hair loss.
The phase 2a hair trial did not show a statistically significant improvement over placebo.
How it works: Blocks CRTH2 (DP2) so PGD2, which is elevated in balding scalp, cannot signal through it.
Risks and caveats: Early trials reported no severe adverse effects distinguishable from placebo; it is unapproved and not marketed.
deepLead:
Setipiprant (ACT-129968, later KYTH-105) is an investigational oral drug that selectively blocks the DP2 (CRTH2) receptor for prostaglandin D2. It was developed by Actelion for asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis, then taken up for androgenetic alopecia after a 2012 finding that PGD2 is elevated in balding scalp.
A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2a trial in men with androgenetic alopecia finished in 2018 without a statistically significant improvement over placebo, according to Wikipedia. The drug is not approved for any use.

name: Ritlecitinib (Litfulo)

angle.text: Ritlecitinib is a prescription drug for severe alopecia areata, where it is used to regrow hair lost in patches. Hair-loss communities discuss it mainly as a separate condition from pattern baldness. It is not studied or approved for pattern hair loss.

summary: Prescription JAK3 inhibitor for severe alopecia areata, not for pattern baldness, and with a boxed warning.
note: Approved only for severe alopecia areata; boxed warning for infections, malignancy, cardiovascular events and thrombosis.
currentQuick:
Ritlecitinib (Litfulo) is a daily pill from Pfizer approved in 2023 for severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune hair loss condition, in people 12 and older.
It is not approved for ordinary male or female pattern hair loss, and no published trial has tested it there, so its relevance to cosmetic hair goals is limited.
How it works: It irreversibly blocks JAK3 and TEC-family kinases, dampening immune signalling involved in the attack on hair follicles, although the label says the importance of each target to its effect is not known.
Risks and caveats: The label carries a boxed warning for serious infections, mortality, malignancy, major cardiovascular events and thrombosis. Common effects include headache, diarrhea and acne. It is prescription only and reportedly costs about US$49,000 a year.
deepLead:
Ritlecitinib, sold as Litfulo and developed by Pfizer, is an oral kinase inhibitor prescribed for severe alopecia areata, an autoimmune condition in which the immune system attacks hair follicles, in adults and adolescents aged 12 and older. The US label describes it as irreversibly inhibiting Janus kinase 3 (JAK3) and the TEC family of kinases, and notes that the relevance of inhibiting specific enzymes to its therapeutic effect is not currently known.
It was first approved by the US FDA in June 2023, followed by the European Union in September 2023 and Canada in November 2023. It is a prescription-only drug and is not indicated for androgenetic (pattern) hair loss, the form of hair loss most discussed in looksmaxxing communities. Its label carries a boxed warning covering serious infections, mortality, malignancy, major adverse cardiovascular events and thrombosis.

name: Verteporfin hair

angle.text: Forum posters discuss verteporfin as a way to regrow follicles in transplant scars and to heal cosmetic surgery without visible scarring. It is an eye-disease drug with lab research on the Hippo pathway. The appearance use rests on lab and anecdotal data.

summary: Eye-disease photosensitizer that forums eye for scarless hair transplants; only lab and anecdotal data support that use.
note: Approved only as an intravenous light-activated eye therapy; hair use is experimental and unstudied in controlled trials.
currentQuick:
Verteporfin is a prescription drug used with a red laser to treat abnormal eye blood vessels. Online hair communities are interested because lab studies suggest it can block a signalling pathway tied to scarring.
Its use for hair transplant scars or follicle regrowth is experimental. Evidence is limited to mouse studies and a few surgeon-reported cases discussed on forums.
How it works: In its approved use it is activated by light to generate reactive oxygen species that close abnormal vessels. In the research relevant to scarring, it is thought to inhibit YAP/TEAD signalling, which affects how fibroblasts respond to injury.
Risks and caveats: The label warns of photosensitivity, extravasation, vision changes and anaphylaxis for the approved eye use. Safety for scalp use has not been studied in controlled trials.
deepLead:
Verteporfin (brand name Visudyne) is a light-activated drug approved for photodynamic therapy of abnormal blood vessels in the eye, for example in wet age-related macular degeneration, pathologic myopia and presumed ocular histoplasmosis. Separately, laboratory research has examined it as an inhibitor of the YAP-TEAD interaction in the Hippo signalling pathway.
In looksmaxxing communities, verteporfin is discussed as an experimental way to reduce scarring and to regenerate hair follicles in scarred or donor areas after hair transplant surgery, a use some posters describe as a route to repeated transplants. This use is not an approved indication, and the human evidence for hair is limited to a few clinician-reported cases discussed online rather than controlled trials.

name: Oral cyproterone acetate

angle.text: Cyproterone acetate is a prescription antiandrogen used in some countries by women for androgen-related scalp hair loss, acne and excess facial or body hair. Users value it for fuller hair and clearer skin. It is labelled or used off-label for these purposes.

summary: Prescription antiandrogen used abroad for women's hair loss, acne and hirsutism, with liver, clot and meningioma risks.
note: Not marketed in the US; EMA warned in 2020 about meningioma at doses of 25 mg/day or more.
currentQuick:
Oral cyproterone acetate is a hormonal drug that blocks androgen receptors and acts as a progestin. In Europe and elsewhere it is prescribed to women for acne, excess hair growth and androgen-related scalp hair loss, often in a pill with ethinylestradiol.
It is not sold in the US and is generally considered impractical for men because of its hormonal effects.
How it works: It blocks androgen receptors, suppresses pituitary gonadotropins through its progestogenic action and so lowers androgen production, and is broken down mainly by the liver enzyme CYP3A4.
Risks and caveats: Documented risks include liver toxicity, venous blood clots, meningioma (EMA warning, 2020) and adrenal insufficiency on abrupt stop of high doses. Pregnancy, liver disease and prior clots are contraindications. It is prescription only.
deepLead:
Cyproterone acetate (CPA) is a steroidal antiandrogen and progestin sold alone as Androcur and, combined with ethinylestradiol, as Diane-35, Dianette and similar products. For hair, it is used in some countries as an off-label or labelled treatment for scalp hair loss, hirsutism, acne and seborrhea in women with androgen-related signs.
It was first synthesised at Schering in 1961 and reached the market as an antiandrogen in Europe in 1973; it has never been marketed in the United States. Documented risks include liver toxicity, blood clots and meningioma, and the European Medicines Agency issued a warning in 2020 about meningioma at higher doses. Because of its effects on male hormones, use for hair loss in men is described as generally impractical.

name: Nutrafol

angle.text: Nutrafol is taken by people with thinning hair, mostly women, who want thicker, fuller-looking hair. It is promoted for anti-inflammatory and DHT-related actions. Several small trials have reported positive results, and the evidence base is rated cautiously.

summary: Branded botanical hair supplement with several small positive trials, mostly in women, and a cautiously rated evidence base.
note: Dietary supplement, not a DHT-blocking drug; trials are small and short.
currentQuick:
Nutrafol is a branded capsule of plant extracts and nutrients sold for thinning hair. Several small, mostly six-month studies in women, menopausal women and some men report more hairs per area than placebo or baseline.
A 2023 systematic review included it among supplements with the highest-quality evidence of possible benefit, with the caution that the research base is limited.
How it works: The product's papers say its Synergen Complex of standardized botanicals targets stress hormones, inflammation, oxidative stress and DHT. Those mechanisms have not been shown in large independent trials.
Risks and caveats: Trials report few or no adverse events, and a systematic review called supplement side effects rare and mild. It is sold as a dietary supplement, not an approved drug.
deepLead:
Nutrafol is a branded multi-ingredient oral supplement marketed for hair thinning. Its published trials describe a proprietary Synergen Complex of standardized botanicals said to have anti-inflammatory, adaptogenic, antioxidant and dihydrotestosterone-inhibiting properties.
Several small randomised and open-label studies of Nutrafol formulations in women, menopausal women, women on plant-based diets and mixed groups have reported increases in hair counts or improved self-assessment. A 2023 JAMA Dermatology systematic review of nutritional supplements for hair loss in people without known deficiency listed Nutrafol among interventions with the highest-quality evidence of potential benefit, while cautioning that its findings should be interpreted carefully.

name: Viviscal

angle.text: Viviscal is taken by men and women with thinning hair who want more density and thickness. It is promoted as a marine protein complex that supports hair growth. A few placebo-controlled trials exist, and one review is cautiously positive.

summary: Marine-protein hair supplement with a few placebo-controlled trials, and a cautiously positive review.
note: Dietary supplement; trials are small and short.
currentQuick:
Viviscal is a marine-protein supplement taken twice daily for thinning hair. Small placebo-controlled trials in women and in men with male pattern hair loss report more terminal hairs and less shedding.
A 2023 systematic review listed it among supplements with the best-quality evidence of possible benefit, with a general caution about the field.
How it works: Its marine complex is proposed to support the hair growth cycle, but human mechanistic evidence is limited.
Risks and caveats: Trials report few or no adverse events, and a systematic review described supplement adverse effects as rare and mild. It is sold as a dietary supplement.
deepLead:
Viviscal is a branded oral supplement built around a marine protein complex, marketed for thinning hair in women and men. Its formulations include Extra Strength and Man versions.
Published placebo-controlled trials of Viviscal products, in women and in men with male pattern hair loss, report more terminal hairs and less shedding than placebo. A 2023 JAMA Dermatology systematic review counted Viviscal among supplements with the highest-quality evidence of potential benefit in people without known deficiency, while advising cautious interpretation.

name: Marine collagen / hair vitamins

angle.text: People take marine collagen and hair vitamin blends hoping for thicker hair, less shedding and a healthier look. Formulations vary widely. A few trials are registered, and little outcome data has been published.

summary: Collagen-and-vitamin hair supplements: a loose product category with small registered trials and little published outcome data.
note: Formulas differ by brand; trial results for one product do not transfer to others.
currentQuick:
Marine collagen and hair vitamins are oral supplements sold to support hair thickness and reduce shedding. They are a broad category, usually combining collagen peptides with vitamins, minerals and plant extracts.
Several small trials of specific products have been registered, but published outcome evidence was not available in the sources reviewed.
How it works: Makers generally propose that supplying collagen-derived peptides and micronutrients supports the hair follicle and hair shaft. The sources reviewed do not establish a mechanism.
Risks and caveats: Safety depends on each product's ingredients. No safety data were available in the sources reviewed; supplements are not regulated like prescription drugs.
deepLead:
Marine collagen and "hair vitamin" products are oral dietary supplements marketed for hair thickness, shedding and general hair health. Formulations vary widely and commonly combine collagen peptides, often sourced from fish, with vitamins, minerals and botanical extracts.
Published evidence for these multi-ingredient products is limited in the sources reviewed here. Several small, mostly single-product trials of hair supplements have been registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, including studies in people with hair thinning and shedding , but this article does not report outcomes for them because results were not available in the sources used.

name: Castor oil hair

angle.text: Castor oil is a traditional home practice applied to the scalp, brows and lashes for thicker, longer-looking hair. Users also value it as a conditioner that adds shine. No clinical trial of it for hair growth was found.

summary: A traditional oil applied to the scalp for hair growth, with no clinical trial for that use found.
note: Hair-growth claims are untested in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Castor oil is a thick plant oil, mostly ricinoleic acid, long used as a laxative and in cosmetics. People apply it to the scalp hoping for thicker or faster-growing hair.
No published clinical trial of castor oil for hair growth was found in the sources reviewed.
How it works: Proponents describe it as moisturizing and nourishing the scalp. No mechanism for hair growth was established in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: The oil itself has had its ricin deactivated in processing. The sources reviewed did not cover scalp-specific adverse effects.
deepLead:
Castor oil is a vegetable oil pressed from the seeds of Ricinus communis. About 90 percent of its triglycerides is ricinoleic acid, a hydroxylated fatty acid . Applying it to the scalp and hair is a popular home practice, and it is promoted for hair growth and thickness.
Wikipedia's article on castor oil, which covers its cosmetic and medicinal uses, does not describe hair-growth research . No published clinical trial of castor oil for hair growth was found in the sources reviewed.

name: Garlic / ginseng / aloe scalp remedies

angle.text: Garlic, ginseng and aloe vera are used as folk scalp remedies by people who want to slow hair loss or improve scalp condition. They are applied as raw preparations, gels or in commercial products. No hair-growth trials were found for these uses.

summary: Folk plant remedies for the scalp, with no hair-growth trials found and documented burn reports for raw garlic.
note: Raw garlic on skin has been linked to burns.
currentQuick:
Garlic, ginseng and aloe vera are among the plant ingredients people apply to the scalp as home remedies for hair loss.
The sources reviewed contain no hair-growth studies of them.
How it works: Users apply juices, gels or extracts to the scalp, usually describing a stimulating or soothing effect. No mechanism for hair growth was established in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia reports burns from topical garlic and possible rash or allergy from aloe gel. Ginseng has listed side effects when taken orally.
deepLead:
Garlic, ginseng and aloe vera are plant-based ingredients that circulate as folk or natural topical remedies for hair loss and scalp health, applied as raw preparations, juices, gels or in commercial products.
The Wikipedia articles on each plant do not describe hair-growth research . They do document safety points relevant to topical use, notably burns reported from topical garlic .

name: Black seed oil hair

chain: Nigella oil on scalp or oral
angle.text: Black seed oil is promoted in some communities for thicker hair and less loss, applied to the scalp or taken orally. Its thymoquinone content is the usual reason cited. Research on it has centred on other conditions, and none was found on hair.

summary: Nigella sativa oil promoted for hair, with research on it centred on other conditions and none found on hair.
note: No hair-specific human studies found.
currentQuick:
Black seed oil comes from Nigella sativa seeds and has a long folk-medicine history. Some people use it for hair growth or thickness.
The sources reviewed contain no hair studies; the research on it covers other conditions and laboratory work on thymoquinone.
How it works: Its main active compound is thymoquinone, studied mostly for anti-inflammatory and anticancer effects in the lab. A hair mechanism was not established in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: The FDA classifies the plant as generally recognized as safe as a spice or flavoring; this concerns food use, and the sources reviewed did not cover safety of the oil on the scalp.
deepLead:
Black seed oil is pressed from the seeds of Nigella sativa, also called black cumin. Its best-known constituent is thymoquinone . It is promoted in some communities for hair thickness and loss, often applied to the scalp or taken orally.
The sources reviewed contain no hair studies of black seed oil. Published research on it concerns other conditions, and Wikipedia notes insufficient high-quality clinical evidence that the seeds or oil treat human diseases .

name: Hair growth shampoo with DHT blockers

chain: Shampoo with ketoconazole or saw palmetto
angle.text: Users add ketoconazole or saw palmetto shampoos to hair routines to support density against androgenetic alopecia. They are an easy low-effort add-on to drug treatments. Evidence for the ingredients in this role is limited.

summary: Shampoos with ketoconazole or saw palmetto sold for hair loss, with limited ingredient-level evidence.
note: Evidence mostly concerns ketoconazole; saw palmetto hair data were not found.
currentQuick:
These shampoos add ingredients like ketoconazole or saw palmetto and are sold to counter hair loss.
Evidence is limited: ketoconazole has some supportive findings, while saw palmetto's evidence concerns the prostate.
How it works: Ketoconazole is an antifungal thought to lower scalp inflammation. Saw palmetto is claimed to reduce DHT, which was not described in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Topical ketoconazole is listed with redness; serious effects relate to oral forms.
deepLead:
Shampoos marketed as DHT blockers typically contain ingredients such as ketoconazole or saw palmetto, positioned as supporting hair against androgenetic alopecia. The sources reviewed describe the evidence for these ingredients as limited.
Wikipedia states that ketoconazole shampoo has been used off-label alongside oral 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, with limited clinical evidence that it may reduce hair loss in some cases .

name: Hair loss concealing hat/cap

angle.text: Caps, hats and beanies are worn to cover thinning hair or baldness, so the scalp is hidden straight away. Users pick styles that suit their face and outfit. The effect is visible while worn and does not treat the hair loss.

summary: Caps and beanies that hide thinning hair without treating it.
note: Tight headwear is linked to traction alopecia.
currentQuick:
Hats and caps cover thinning areas of the scalp. They are a concealment option that leaves the underlying hair unchanged.
No studies of hats as a hair-loss concealment were found.
How it works: The hat physically covers the scalp.
Risks and caveats: Tight or compressive headwear worn for long periods is associated with traction alopecia.
deepLead:
Caps, hats and beanies are worn to cover thinning hair or baldness. They conceal rather than treat hair loss.
Wikipedia notes that tight headwear can cause traction alopecia, a mechanical form of hair loss distinct from androgenetic baldness .
